title: About me
text:
About me

PhD Candidate · Political Science · Aarhus University
Welcome to my website! My name is Mads, and I am a PhD candidate in Political Science at Aarhus University. My research examines how citizens perceive and evaluate their political representatives – with a particular focus on the social and professional backgrounds of politicians and what these mean for political support.
In my PhD dissertation, I use survey experiments and quantitative text analysis to study how perceptions of political elites shape political trust, feelings of representation, and democratic satisfaction among ordinary citizens.

title: Mads Nørgaard
text:
Working Papers

The Political Class in Citizens’ Minds: Mapping Public Perceptions of Politicians
Available upon request

Abstract
Politicians are often portrayed as a socially distinct and internally homogeneous elite -- a narrative central to populist rhetoric and scholarly debates on political discontent. Yet we know little about how voters mentally represent politicians. Using survey data from Denmark (N=1,302), combining free association tasks, open-ended descriptions, and closed-ended items, I demonstrate that most citizens view politicians as both internally homogeneous and socially distinct from the general population. These perceptions correlate with negative characterisations and significantly lower political trust, external efficacy, and democratic satisfaction. Crucially, perceived social distinctiveness matters more than perceived homogeneity: citizens who view politicians as different from ordinary people show substantially diminished political support, regardless of whether they see politicians as similar to one another. By shifting analytical focus from objective elite characteristics to citizens’ mental representations, this study highlights the importance of not only who politicians are, but how they are imagined by the public.

Too Professional to Represent? Perceptions of Politicians’ Careers and Feelings of Representation
Available upon request

Abstract
 A common concern in contemporary politics is that politicians are increasingly detached from the population. Central to this critique is the claim that politicians lack 'real-world' experience. Yet, little is known about citizens' perceptions of politicians' career background, or how these affect political support. Using an original survey from Denmark (N = 1.712), this paper documents a widespread conception of politicians as lacking extra-political experience. A pre-registered experiment further demonstrates that even subtle priming of these considerations reduces political support, whereas receiving new information does not produce a corresponding increase. Finally, analysis of open-ended responses shows that respondents who perceive MPs as lacking experience are more likely to question the information they receive, suggesting that perceptions of politicians -- and the consequences thereof -- may be rooted more in citizens’ feelings and culturally available narratives than in objective reality.
